mainTopic: Old age in קהלת and in stories of the חכמים, the value of youth, and teachings about death and mourning
overview: This amud is mostly about old age and what comes after it. The גמרא reads the last chapter of קהלת phrase by phrase as a picture of the aging body: ribs, legs, teeth, eyes, stomach, sleep, hearing, and desire. Stories bring the verses to life. רבי יהושע בן חנניה tells the emperor in a riddle that he is too old to debate, and רבי שמעון בן חלפתא tells רבי that rocks now seem tall and his two legs have become three. Sayings about youth teach that it is precious and never returns, and that one should eat well while young. In between, רבי יהושע בן קרחה answers a mocking eunuch insult for insult. ברזילי's words to דוד add more signs of aging. רב says ברזילי was lying, and רבא says he really aged early. A ברייתא teaches that Torah scholars grow wiser with age. The amud ends with death: each צדיק gets his own place in the next world, the soul mourns for seven days, and רב יהודה rules that ten people sit in place of mourners for someone who has none. That story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Which tears hurt the eyes and which help them
steps.stepSummary: This finishes a list from the previous section. Tears from straining in the bathroom are bad for the eyes. Tears from medicine, laughter, or sharp produce are good.
steps.simpleTranslation: And tears from the bathroom are bad. Tears from medicine, from laughter, and from sharp fruits are good.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a list that started on the previous amud. It sorts tears into ones that harm the eyes and ones that help them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tears that come from strain or pain, like straining in the bathroom, weaken the eyes. Tears that come from something healthy (medicine), something happy (laughter), or something sharp (strong produce) are good for the eyes. The eyes connect to the next step, where 'those who look out the windows' are also explained as the eyes.

phrases.english: And those (tears) of the bathroom are bad.
phrases.notes: This continues a list on the previous amud, which began with harmful kinds of tears.

phrases.english: Those from medicine and those from laughter,
and those from (sharp) produce are good.
phrases.notes: 'Good' means good for the eyes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends a list of tears that began earlier.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tears from the bathroom harm the eyes. Tears from medicine, laughter, and sharp produce benefit them.

steps.title: קהלת's verse explained as the aging body
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads קהלת 12:3 as a description of the body in old age. Each phrase of the verse is matched to a body part.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'On the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men bow down...' The keepers of the house are the flanks and ribs. The strong men are the legs. The grinders that stop are the teeth. The ones looking out the windows that grow dark are the eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a verse from קהלת and explains each image in it as a body part that weakens in old age.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse describes a 'house' falling apart, and the body is that house. The ribs guard it, the legs carry its strength, the teeth 'grind' food, and the eyes 'look out the windows.' This explanation sets up the next story, where רבי יהושע בן חנניה uses the same kind of picture language.

keyTerms.meaning: Keepers of the house (here, the ribs and flanks)
Windows (the eyes look out of them)

steps.whyThisMatters: This reading of the verse is the key to understanding רבי יהושע בן חנניה's riddle in the next steps.

phrases.english: "On the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble,
and (the strong men) shall bow down, etc."
phrases.notes: קהלת 12:3. The 'etc.' stands for the rest of the verse, which is explained below.

phrases.english: "On the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble":
these are the flanks and the ribs.
phrases.notes: They surround and protect the organs inside the body.

phrases.english: "And the strong men shall bow down": these are the legs.
"And the grinders shall cease": these are the teeth.
"And those that look out the windows shall be darkened": these are the eyes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the explanation of verses in קהלת about old age.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In קהלת 12:3, the ribs, legs, teeth, and eyes are described as parts of a 'house' that wears out with age.

steps.title: The emperor asks why the sage stopped coming
steps.stepSummary: The Roman emperor asks רבי יהושע בן חנניה why he no longer comes to the בי אבידן, the place where debates were held.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor said to רבי יהושע בן חנניה: Why don't you come to the House of Avidan anymore?
steps.whatsHappening: A story begins. The emperor asks a question, which sets up רבי יהושע בן חנניה's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן חנניה used to take part in debates at the בי אבידן. The emperor wants to know why he stopped. The answer will tie back to the aging body from the verse in קהלת.

keyTerms.meaning: House of Avidan, a meeting place for debates

phrases.english: The emperor said to him,
to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya:
What is the reason you do not come
to the House of Avidan?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ קֵיסָר לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a story that acts out the aging described in the verse in קהלת.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי יהושע בן חנניה stopped coming to the debates.

steps.title: The riddle: the snowy mountain
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן חנניה answers with a riddle. His hair is white like snow, his voice is weak like dogs that don't bark, and his teeth no longer grind.
steps.simpleTranslation: He answered: The snowy mountain is surrounded by ice. Its dogs don't bark. Its grinders don't grind.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן חנניה answers the emperor in picture language, saying he has grown too old.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'snowy mountain' is his white head of hair. 'Dogs that don't bark' means his voice can no longer be heard, which matters in a debate. 'Grinders that don't grind' are his teeth, the same picture as 'the grinders cease' in קהלת.
steps.confusionAlert: He is not speaking about a real mountain or real dogs. Each image is a body part, just like in the verse in קהלת.

phrases.english: He said to him:
The snowy mountain is surrounded by ice.
phrases.notes: His hair and beard have turned white.

phrases.english: Its dogs do not bark.
phrases.notes: His voice can no longer be heard.

phrases.english: Its grinders do not grind.
phrases.notes: His teeth have fallen out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the emperor's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is too old: white-haired, weak-voiced, and toothless.

steps.title: בי רב adds: searching for what I never lost
steps.stepSummary: The students of רב add a line to his answer: 'I am searching for what I did not lose.' This describes an old man who walks bent over.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רב says he also said: What I have not lost, I am searching for.
steps.whatsHappening: The students of רב report one more line in רבי יהושע בן חנניה's answer, about walking bent over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An old man walks hunched over and looking at the ground, as if he is hunting for something he dropped. This adds one more sign of old age to the riddle.

phrases.english: The school of Rav says (he added):
What I have not lost, I am searching for.
phrases.notes: He walks bent over, as if looking for something.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another line to the answer in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An old man's bent walk looks like searching for something lost.

steps.title: Two is better than three
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר קיסמא says two legs (youth) are better than three (old age with a cane). He also mourns 'the one that goes and does not come back.'
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא: רבי יוסי בר קיסמא says: Two are better than three. Woe to the one that leaves and does not return.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching about old age is brought from a ברייתא. Its second half is a riddle that the next step will ask about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'two' are a young person's two legs, and the 'three' are an old person's two legs plus a cane. The phrase 'the one that goes and does not come back' is unclear, so it sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
Goes and does not come back

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר קִיסְמָא אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Yosei bar Kisma says:
Two are better than three.
phrases.notes: Two legs in youth compared with two legs and a cane in old age.

phrases.english: Woe for the one
that goes and does not come back.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר קִיסְמָא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the story to a new saying about the value of youth.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Youth is better than old age, and there is something precious that leaves and never returns.

steps.title: What is the thing that never returns?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'the one that goes and does not come back' means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to explain רבי יוסי בר קיסמא's riddle. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'the one that goes and does not come back' do not say what they refer to. The גמרא wants to know exactly what is being mourned.

phrases.english: What is it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the riddle in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What 'the one that goes and does not come back' refers to.

steps.title: רב חסדא: it is youth
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא explains that the thing that leaves and never returns is youth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: Youth.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers the question: the thing that is gone forever is youth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Strength and health can come back after an illness, but youth never comes back once it is gone. That is why רבי יוסי בר קיסמא said 'woe' about it.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
Youth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The thing that leaves and never returns is youth.

steps.title: A crown of roses and a crown of thorns
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי says youth is like a crown of roses, and old age is like a crown of thorns.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said: Youth is a crown of roses. Old age is a crown of thorns.
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי adds another saying that compares youth with old age.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Youth is beautiful and pleasant, like a crown of roses. Old age is painful and hard, like a crown of thorns. This fits with רב חסדא's point that youth is precious.

keyTerms.meaning: When (he) came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came, he said:
Youth is a crown of roses;
old age is a crown of thorns.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second image about how precious youth is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Youth is pleasant like roses; old age is painful like thorns.

steps.title: Chew well and your legs will be strong
steps.stepSummary: In the name of רבי מאיר: chew your food well with your teeth, and you will find strength in your legs. A verse in ירמיהו is brought as support.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in the name of רבי מאיר: Grind with your teeth and you will find it in your feet. As it says: 'We ate our fill of bread, we were well, and we saw no evil.'
steps.whatsHappening: Advice is given in the name of רבי מאיר about eating well to keep the body strong, with a verse brought to support it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating well and chewing thoroughly gives the body strength to carry itself. The verse links being full of bread with being healthy. This connects to the earlier images of teeth (grinders) and legs (strong men) that weaken with age.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in the name of
As it is said (introduces a verse)

phrases.english: It was taught in the name of Rabbi Meir:
Grind with your teeth and you will find (it) in your feet,
phrases.notes: Chewing well gives the legs strength.

phrases.english: as it is said: "We were full of bread, and we were well,
and we saw no evil."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 44:17.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from mourning youth to advice for keeping strong.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating well and chewing properly gives the body strength.

steps.title: שמואל: eat while young, drink when older
steps.stepSummary: שמואל tells רב יהודה to eat now. Until age forty food is good for you, and after forty drink is better.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said to רב יהודה: Sharp one, open your sack and put in your bread. Until forty, eating helps. From then on, drinking helps.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives רב יהודה practical advice to eat well while young, then explains how food and drink matter at different ages. This closes the group of sayings about youth before the גמרא turns to a different story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Open your sack' means open your mouth and eat. Until forty, solid food builds the body. After forty, drink is more helpful.

keyTerms.meaning: Sharp one / big-toothed one (a nickname for רב יהודה)

steps.whatToRemember: This section paints old age as the body's 'house' wearing out: ribs, legs, teeth, and eyes. Youth is precious and never returns. The practical advice is to eat well while young, since food helps until forty and drink helps after that.

phrases.english: Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda:
Sharp one, open your sack
phrases.notes: The 'sack' is the mouth.

phrases.english: and put in your bread.
Until forty years, food is beneficial;
from then on, drink is beneficial.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the advice on eating, adding when food and drink help most.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eat well while young. Food benefits the body until forty, and drink benefits it afterward.

steps.title: The eunuch asks a mocking question about distance
steps.stepSummary: A eunuch asks רבי יהושע בן קרחה how far it is to a town called Karchina. The name hints at baldness. The חכם answers with a town whose name hints at castration.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain eunuch said to רבי יהושע בן קרחה: How far is it from here to Karchina? He answered: The same as from here to Gozenya.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story of insults dressed up as innocent questions. The eunuch hints that the רבי is bald, and the רבי hints right back that the eunuch is castrated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Karchina sounds like קרח, meaning bald, and it also plays on the רבי's own name, קרחה. Gozenya sounds like גוזא, meaning castrated. The answer 'the same distance' means: my flaw is no bigger than yours.

keyTerms.meaning: A eunuch (castrated man); here, a hostile apostate
A place name that hints at קֵרֵחַ (bald)
A place name that hints at גּוֹזָא (castrated)
How much is it? (here: how far)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a real question about travel. Both the question and the answer are wordplay insults built on place names.

phrases.english: A certain eunuch said to him
to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha:
From here to Karchina, how far is it?
phrases.notes: This is a hint at going bald.

phrases.english: He said to him: The same as from here to Gozenya.
phrases.notes: This is a hint at castration.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא גּוֹזָאָה לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from sayings about aging and the body to a story about bodily flaws
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A mocking hint at baldness is answered with a matching hint at castration

steps.title: Bald goat versus castrated goat
steps.stepSummary: The eunuch says a bald goat sells for four. The רבי replies that a castrated goat sells for eight.
steps.simpleTranslation: The eunuch said: A bald buck sells for four. The רבי said: A castrated goat sells for eight.
steps.whatsHappening: The insults move from place names to animal prices. Each man compares the other to a cheap, flawed goat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The eunuch calls the רבי a bald goat worth only four. The רבי answers that a castrated goat goes for eight. On one reading, a castrated goat fetches more because it fattens up, so the jab still lands: the eunuch is like an animal raised to be eaten.

keyTerms.meaning: A castrated goat (literally, with its root pulled out)

phrases.english: He said to him: A bald buck goes for four.
He said to him: A castrated goat goes for eight.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second round of the same exchange of insults
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The bald-goat insult is turned back with a castrated-goat insult

steps.title: The eunuch mocks the רבי for walking barefoot
steps.stepSummary: The eunuch sees that the רבי has no shoes. He ranks people by how they travel and says a barefoot man is worse than a dead man.
steps.simpleTranslation: He saw that the רבי was not wearing shoes. He said: Whoever rides a horse is a king, whoever rides a donkey is a free man, and whoever has shoes on his feet is at least a human being. Whoever has none of these, someone dead and buried is better off than him.
steps.whatsHappening: The eunuch opens a new insult. He builds a ladder of status and puts the barefoot רבי below the dead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three levels: horse means king, donkey means free man, and shoes mean a basic human being. Having none of them puts a person beneath even someone in the grave. This list of three sets up the רבי's reply of three in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A human being, a proper person
One who is dug in and buried (dead)

phrases.english: He saw that he was not wearing his shoes,
he said to him: One on a horse is a king,
one on a donkey is a free man,
and one with shoes on his feet is a human being.
One who has neither this nor that,
one who is dug in and buried is better than him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The eunuch launches a fresh, sharper insult
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A barefoot person is mocked as lower than the dead

steps.title: The רבי answers three insults with three of his own
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה names three blessings a eunuch can never have: a beard, a wife, and children. He then thanks ה׳, mockingly, for denying the eunuch all of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Eunuch, eunuch, you said three things to me, now hear three. The glory of the face is a beard. The joy of the heart is a wife. 'The portion of ה׳ is children.' Blessed is the Omnipresent who kept all of them from you.
steps.whatsHappening: The רבי replies with a matching list of three. Each item is something a eunuch lacks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The eunuch ranked people by status symbols. The רבי ranks them by real blessings: a beard, a wife, and children, the last taken from a פסוק in תהלים. Since a eunuch has none of the three, the barefoot insult flips back on him.

keyTerms.meaning: The Omnipresent, a name for ה׳

phrases.english: He said to him: Eunuch, eunuch,
you said three to me, now hear three:
the glory of the face is a beard,
the joy of the heart is a wife,
'the portion of ה׳ is children.'
phrases.notes: תהלים קכז:ג

phrases.english: Blessed is the Omnipresent who denied you all of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוֹזָא גּוֹזָא, תְּלָת אֲמַרְתְּ לִי, תְּלָת שָׁמְעַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A direct, matching reply to the eunuch's three-part insult
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A eunuch lacks a beard, a wife, and children, which are the true blessings

steps.title: Final jabs: who is fit to argue or rebuke
steps.stepSummary: The eunuch asks whether a bald man has any business quarreling. The רבי answers: does a castrated goat have any business rebuking?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: A bald man quarrels?! He answered: A castrated goat gives rebuke?!
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with one last pair of jabs. The רבי gets the final word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The eunuch says a bald man should not pick fights. The רבי answers that a castrated goat has no standing to rebuke anyone, and the eunuch is the one who started the attack. The pattern of the whole story holds to the end: every insult comes straight back.
steps.whatToRemember: In every round, רבי יהושע בן קרחה answers the eunuch's mockery with an equal or sharper reply about the eunuch's own condition.

phrases.english: He said to him: A bald man quarrels?!
He said to him: A castrated goat gives rebuke?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the exchange of insults
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The eunuch has no standing to rebuke anyone

steps.title: רבי asks why רבי שמעון בן חלפתא stopped visiting
steps.stepSummary: רבי asks politely why they did not get to greet רבי שמעון בן חלפתא on the festival, as their fathers used to greet each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי said to רבי שמעון בן חלפתא: Why did we not greet you on the festival, the way my fathers greeted your fathers?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the theme of old age with a new story. This question sets up the answer that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי is really asking why רבי שמעון בן חלפתא did not come to visit him. He phrases it gently, as if the failure were his own. He mentions the family tradition to show that the visit was expected.

keyTerms.meaning: We greeted you, we received your presence

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן חֲלַפְתָּא:
phrases.english: Rabbi said to Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta:

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי מָה לֹא הִקְבַּלְנוּ פָּנֶיךָ בָּרֶגֶל,
phrases.english: For what reason did we not greet you on the festival,
the way my fathers greeted your fathers?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִפְּנֵי מָה לֹא הִקְבַּלְנוּ פָּנֶיךָ בָּרֶגֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story that returns to the theme of old age
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי שמעון בן חלפתא did not come to visit on the festival

steps.title: Old age in four short images
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן חלפתא explains that old age keeps him home. Rocks seem tall, near places seem far, he walks with a cane, and his marital desire is gone.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: The rocks have become tall, near places have become far, two have become three, and the one who makes peace in the house is gone.
steps.whatsHappening: He answers רבי's question by describing what old age has done to his body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Small rocks now feel like walls, and short trips feel long. His two legs have become three because he needs a cane. 'What makes peace in the home' refers to the marital drive, which no longer works for him.

keyTerms.meaning: Two have become three (two legs plus a cane)
What brings peace to the home (the marital drive)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Two became three' is not about numbers or people. It means his two legs now need a walking stick.

phrases.english: He said to him: Rocks have become tall,
near places have become far,
two have become three,
the one who makes peace in the house has ceased.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Old age has made travel too hard for him, and his body no longer functions as it did

steps.title: Shut doors and the quiet mill: body openings and the stomach
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads קהלת יב:ד as a picture of aging. The 'shut doors' are the body's openings, and the 'low sound of the mill' is a stomach that no longer digests.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And the doors shall be shut in the marketplace': these are a person's orifices. 'When the sound of the grinding is low': because the stomach does not grind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to explaining the פסוקים of קהלת פרק יב one phrase at a time, with each phrase standing for a part of the aging body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'doors' are the body's openings, which stop working normally. The 'mill' is the stomach. When it stops grinding food well, its 'sound' grows quiet.

keyTerms.meaning: And the doors shall be shut

phrases.english: 'And the doors shall be shut in the marketplace, etc.'
These are the orifices of a person.
'When the sound of the mill is low'
because the stomach does not grind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the phrase-by-phrase reading of קהלת on old age
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The shut doors are the body's openings, and the quiet mill is a stomach that does not digest

steps.title: Light sleep and lost joy in music
steps.stepSummary: The rest of the פסוק describes an old person who wakes at the sound of a bird and no longer enjoys singing.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And one shall rise at the voice of a bird': even a bird wakes him from his sleep. 'And all the daughters of song shall be brought low': even the voices of male and female singers sound to him like ordinary talk.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining קהלת יב:ד with two more signs of old age.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An old person sleeps so lightly that a bird's chirp wakes him. And he loses his pleasure in music, so beautiful singing sounds like plain conversation.
steps.whatToRemember: The verses of קהלת פרק יב are read as a step-by-step picture of an aging body: the openings, the stomach, sleep, and the enjoyment of music.

phrases.english: 'And one shall rise at the voice of the bird'
for even a bird wakes him from his sleep.
'And all the daughters of song shall be brought low'
for even the voice of male and female singers
seems to him like conversation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same פסוק with its next phrases
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Old age brings very light sleep and a loss of pleasure in song

steps.title: ברזילי's words show how old age affects the mind, mouth, and ears
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings ברזילי הגלעדי's words to דוד (שמואל ב יט:לו) and learns three signs of aging from them: the mind changes, the lips crack, and the ears grow heavy.
steps.simpleTranslation: And also ברזילי הגלעדי said to דוד: 'I am eighty years old today. Can I tell between good and bad?' From here we learn that the minds of old people change. 'Can your servant taste what I eat and what I drink?' From here we learn that the lips of old people crack. 'Can I still hear the voice of singing men and singing women?' From here we learn that the ears of old people become heavy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another source about old age, the words of ברזילי, and learns one sign of aging from each of his three phrases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 19-20 used קהלת to describe aging. Now the גמרא adds a second source from נביא, where a real old man describes himself. Each of his three questions becomes a lesson about a different part of the body: the mind, the mouth, and the ears.

keyTerms.meaning: An old man from Gilead who supported דוד and was invited to live with him in Jerusalem
Crack, wither (the lips lose their sense of taste)

phrases.english: And also Barzilai the Gileadite said to David:
"I am eighty years old today;
can I tell between good and bad?"
From here we learn that the minds of the elderly change.
"Can your servant taste

phrases.aramaic: אֶת אֲשֶׁר אוֹכַל וְאֶת אֲשֶׁר אֶשְׁתֶּה״ —
phrases.english: what I eat and what I drink?"
From here we learn that the lips of the elderly crack and wither.
"Can I still hear the voice of singing men and singing women?"
From here we learn that the ears of the elderly become heavy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second scriptural description of aging, alongside the קהלת verses in steps 19-20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Old age changes the mind, weakens taste, and dulls hearing, as ברזילי describes.

steps.title: רב says ברזילי was lying, since a 92-year-old maid could still taste food
steps.stepSummary: רב says ברזילי was not telling the truth. He points to a maidservant in רבי's house who was 92 and still tasted the cooking pots.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: ברזילי הגלעדי was a liar. For there was a certain maidservant in רבי's house who was ninety-two years old, and she would still taste the pots.
steps.whatsHappening: רב pushes back on ברזילי's description. He says ברזילי only claimed to be too old so he would not have to go with דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's proof comes from real life. If a 92-year-old woman could still taste whether the food was cooked right, an 80-year-old man should be able to taste too. So ברזילי's complaint was an excuse, not a true picture of normal aging.

keyTerms.meaning: The household of רבי יהודה הנשיא

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב: בַּרְזִילַּי הַגִּלְעָדִי שַׁקָּרָא הֲוָה.
phrases.english: Rav said: Barzilai the Gileadite was a liar.
For there was a certain maidservant in Rabbi's house
who was ninety-two years old,
and she would taste the pots.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: בַּרְזִילַּי הַגִּלְעָדִי שַׁקָּרָא הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether ברזילי's words really describe normal aging, using an example from real life.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Normal 80-year-olds do not lose their sense of taste, so ברזילי was making an excuse.

steps.title: רבא says ברזילי spoke truthfully but aged early because of immoral behavior
steps.stepSummary: רבא disagrees with רב. ברזילי really was that weak, because he was steeped in immorality, and such behavior makes a person age early.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: ברזילי הגלעדי was steeped in immorality, and anyone who is steeped in immorality, old age jumps upon him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different explanation. ברזילי was not lying. He really aged before his time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא accepts רב's point that a normal 80-year-old can still taste. But he explains ברזילי's case as an exception: his behavior made him age early. So his words were true about himself, even if they are not true of every old person.

keyTerms.meaning: Old age jumps upon him (comes early)

steps.confusionAlert: רבא does not argue with רב about the maidservant. Both agree normal people can taste at 80. They only disagree about whether ברזילי was lying or was a special case.

phrases.aramaic: רָבָא אָמַר: בַּרְזִילַּי הַגִּלְעָדִי שָׁטוּף בְּזִמָּה הֲוָה,
phrases.english: Rava said: Barzilai the Gileadite was steeped in promiscuity,
and anyone who is steeped in promiscuity —
old age jumps upon him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: בַּרְזִילַּי הַגִּלְעָדִי שָׁטוּף בְּזִמָּה הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to רב's problem, keeping ברזילי truthful by treating him as an exception.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Exceptional cause: ברזילי aged early, so his weakness was real.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ברזילי must have been lying, since normal 80-year-olds can taste (רב).
steps.terutzMaskana: In רבא's view, ברזילי spoke truthfully, because his immoral lifestyle made old age come upon him early. The גמרא does not decide between רב and רבא.

steps.title: Torah scholars grow wiser with age; ignorant people grow more foolish
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא from רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי teaches that aging affects the mind differently depending on Torah learning, with a proof from two פסוקים in איוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי says: Torah scholars, the older they get, the more wisdom is added to them, as it says: 'With the aged is wisdom, and length of days brings understanding.' And ignorant people, the older they get, the more foolishness is added to them, as it says: 'He removes the speech of the trusted ones and takes away the understanding of the elders.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that softens the earlier statement that 'the minds of the elderly change.' It depends on who the old person is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 said old people's minds change. This ברייתא explains that the change goes in two directions. Torah learning makes the mind sharper with age, while a person without Torah grows duller. Each side is supported by its own פסוק in איוב.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא

steps.whatToRemember: Aging does not have to weaken the mind. For תלמידי חכמים, years bring more wisdom.
steps.whyThisMatters: This changes the whole discussion. Old age is not only decline. Torah learning protects and grows the mind.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei says:
Torah scholars, as long as they grow older —
wisdom is added to them,
as it says: "With the aged is wisdom,
and length of days brings understanding."
And ignorant people, as long as they grow older —
foolishness is added to them,
as it says: "He removes the speech of the trusted ones
and takes away the understanding of the elders."

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Refines step 21's statement that the minds of the elderly change.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Aging adds wisdom to תלמידי חכמים and foolishness to עמי הארץ.

steps.title: קהלת's 'fear of heights' and 'terrors on the road' describe an old person walking
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to קהלת יב:ה. 'Afraid of what is high' means a small bump looks like a mountain. 'Terrors on the road' means walking becomes frightening.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'They will also be afraid of what is high' means that even a small bump seems to him like the highest mountains. 'And terrors on the road' means that when he walks on the road, he has fears.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to explaining the קהלת verses about aging, now moving on to the next פסוק, קהלת יב:ה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These two phrases match what רבי שמעון בן חלפתא said in step 18, that rocks seem tall to him. An old person feels small obstacles as huge and is afraid of falling while walking.

keyTerms.meaning: A small bump or mound in the ground

phrases.english: "They will also be afraid of what is high" —
that even a small bump
seems to him like the highest of mountains.
"And terrors on the road" —
when he walks on the road
fears come upon him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the phrase-by-phrase reading of קהלת after the ברזילי side discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קהלת describes how an old person fears small obstacles and walking.

steps.title: The almond, grasshopper, and caper berry stand for the hip, buttocks, and desire
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes explaining the images in קהלת יב:ה: the blossoming almond is the hip bone, the dragging grasshopper is the heavy buttocks, and the failing caper berry is lost desire.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And the almond tree will blossom' is the hip bone. 'And the grasshopper will drag itself along' is the buttocks. 'And the caper berry will fail' is desire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא decodes three nature pictures in the פסוק as parts of an aging body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each picture stands for a physical change. The hip bone sticks out like a blossom, the backside becomes heavy, which the גמרא reads into the word חגב by a wordplay, and desire stops. The last one, desire, sets up the story that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: The buttocks (a wordplay on חָגָב, grasshopper)

phrases.english: "And the almond tree will blossom" — this is the hip bone.
"And the grasshopper will drag itself along" — these are the buttocks.
"And the caper berry will fail" — this is desire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same פסוק, explaining its remaining images.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The images in the פסוק stand for the hip, the buttocks, and the end of desire.

steps.title: רב sighs at the verse, and רב כהנא understands that רב's desire has ended
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא was reading פסוקים before רב. When he reached this verse, רב sighed, and רב כהנא concluded that רב's desire had stopped.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא was reading the verses before רב. When he reached this פסוק, רב sighed. רב כהנא said: Learn from this that רב's desire has ended.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story that shows the verse about lost desire coming true in a real person, רב himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's sigh showed that the verse described what he was feeling. רב כהנא reads the reaction as evidence. The story makes the aging verse personal and real.

keyTerms.meaning: He drew out a breath and sighed

phrases.aramaic: רַב כָּהֲנָא הֲוָה פָּסֵיק סִידְרָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב.
phrases.english: Rav Kahana was reading the verses before Rav.
When he reached this verse,
Rav drew a breath and sighed.
Rav Kahana said: Learn from this
that Rav's desire has ceased.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא הֲוָה פָּסֵיק סִידְרָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the last phrase of step 26, desire failing, happening in רב's own life.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב's sigh at the verse showed that his desire had ended in old age.

steps.title: רב כהנא: God's word created the drive for a wife and children
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא explains תהלים לג:ט. 'He spoke and it was' refers to a wife, and 'He commanded and it stood' refers to children.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: What is meant by what is written, 'For He spoke and it was'? This is a woman. 'He commanded and it stood'? These are children.
steps.whatsHappening: Still on the topic of desire, רב כהנא reads a פסוק in תהלים as describing the natural drive God placed in people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Getting married and raising children takes huge effort that pure logic might avoid. רב כהנא explains that God 'spoke' and 'commanded' a built-in desire, so people do these things anyway. This shows why the end of desire in step 27 is a real change in life.

keyTerms.meaning: What is meant by what is written
And it was (it came to be)

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said: What is meant by that which is written:
"For He spoke and it was" — this is a woman.
"He commanded and it stood" — these are children.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching from רב כהנא on the theme of desire raised in step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God built into people the drive to marry and to raise children.

steps.title: Desire draws people even past what is physically unappealing
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא describes a woman's body in blunt physical terms, yet notes that everyone still chases after her. This shows how strong God-given desire is.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: A woman is a flask full of waste, and her mouth is full of blood, yet everyone runs after her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the topic of desire with a ברייתא that shows how powerful it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא uses blunt, indirect language about the digestive system and the menstrual cycle to describe the body in plain physical terms. Even so, desire overpowers this, which supports רב כהנא's point that the drive comes from God, not from cold logic.
steps.whatToRemember: This whole section shows how strong desire is in life, which is why its fading is such a clear sign of old age.

phrases.english: It was taught: A woman is a flask full of waste,
and her mouth is full of blood —
yet everyone runs after her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 28 by showing that desire is stronger than physical appearance.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Desire is so strong that it overcomes what is physically unappealing, so it must be built in by God.

steps.title: Each righteous person gets a home that fits his honor
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק explains 'his eternal home' to mean that every צדיק receives his own dwelling in the next world, according to his level.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'For a person goes to his eternal home.' רבי יצחק said: This teaches that each and every righteous person is given a dwelling place according to his honor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the same verse from קהלת יב:ה and explains its next words. רבי יצחק reads 'his home' as a personal home for each צדיק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse does not say 'the eternal home.' It says 'HIS eternal home.' רבי יצחק learns from this that every person has his own place in עולם הבא, matched to what he earned.

keyTerms.meaning: According to his honor or level

phrases.english: "For a person goes to his eternal home"
phrases.notes: This is the rest of the verse in קהלת יב:ה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said:
This teaches that each and every righteous person
is given a dwelling place according to his honor.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הוֹלֵךְ הָאָדָם אֶל בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to finish explaining קהלת יב:ה after the side stories about desire.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'His eternal home' teaches that each צדיק gets a personal place in the next world, matched to his level.

steps.title: Parable of the king and his servants entering a city
steps.stepSummary: A parable explains רבי יצחק's idea: everyone enters through one gate, but each one sleeps in a place that fits his rank.
steps.simpleTranslation: A parable: A king enters a city with his servants. When they enter, they all come in through one gate. When they stay for the night, each one is given a place that fits his honor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a parable to make רבי יצחק's teaching easy to picture.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'one gate' is death, which comes to everyone the same way. The 'lodging' is the next world, where each person's place is different. So death is equal for all, but the reward is not.

phrases.english: A parable: a king who enters
he and his servants, into a city.
When they enter,
they all enter through one gate.
phrases.notes: Like death, which is the same for everyone

phrases.english: When they stay for the night,
each and every one is given
a dwelling place according to his honor.
phrases.notes: Like the next world, where rewards differ

steps.triggerLanguage: מָשָׁל לְמֶלֶךְ שֶׁנִּכְנָס הוּא וַעֲבָדָיו לָעִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows step 30's idea through a parable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Everyone dies the same way, but each person's place in the next world is different.

steps.title: Deeds of youth darken a person's face in old age
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק explains 'youth and שחרות' with a play on the word: what a person does when young can 'blacken' his face with shame when he is old.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק said: What is the meaning of the verse 'For childhood and youth are vanity'? Things a person does in his youth darken his face when he grows old.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק gives a second teaching, on a nearby verse in קהלת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word שחרות means 'youth,' but it sounds like שחור, 'black.' רבי יצחק reads it as a warning: wrong things done when young will bring shame later in life.
steps.confusionAlert: שחרות here does not mean 'dawn' or 'morning.' רבי יצחק reads it as 'black,' as in a face darkened by shame.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak said: What is the meaning of what is written:
"For childhood and youth are vanity"
phrases.notes: קהלת יא:י

phrases.english: Things that a person does in his youth
darken his face when he grows old.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching from the same speaker, רבי יצחק, on a nearby verse in קהלת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: What a person does wrong when young brings him shame in old age.

steps.title: Worms hurt the dead like a needle hurts the living
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק teaches that the dead body feels the worms, and brings a proof from a verse in איוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק said: Worms are as painful to a dead person as a needle in living flesh, as it says: 'But his flesh is in pain for him.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק gives a third teaching, this time about what the dead body feels, and backs it up with a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse in איוב speaks about a dead person, yet it says 'his flesh is in pain.' So רבי יצחק learns that a dead body still feels some pain from the worms eating it.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak said:
Worms are as painful to the dead
as a needle in living flesh,
as it says: "But his flesh is in pain for him."
phrases.notes: איוב יד:כב, first half of the verse

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק קָשָׁה רִימָּה לַמֵּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third teaching from רבי יצחק, now about the body after death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dead body feels the worms like a living person feels a needle.

steps.title: The soul mourns for the person for seven days
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא uses the second half of the same verse in איוב, together with a verse about יעקב, to teach that the soul mourns its body for seven days.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: A person's soul mourns for him all seven days, as it says: 'And his soul mourns over him.' And it is written: 'And he made a mourning for his father seven days.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא continues with the rest of the same verse in איוב and teaches how long the soul mourns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse in איוב tells us the soul mourns, but not for how long. The verse about יוסף mourning יעקב uses the same word אבל and says 'seven days.' Putting the two verses together, רב חסדא concludes that the soul's mourning lasts seven days.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
A person's soul mourns for him
all seven days,
as it says: "And his soul mourns over him,"
phrases.notes: איוב יד:כב, second half of the verse from step 33

phrases.english: and it is written: "And he made a mourning for his father seven days."
phrases.notes: בראשית נ:י, יוסף mourning יעקב

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם מִתְאַבֶּלֶת עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the second half of the verse that רבי יצחק quoted in step 33.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The soul mourns for the person for seven days, like the seven days of mourning for a relative.

steps.title: If a dead person has no mourners, ten people sit in his place
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה gives a practical rule: when no one is mourning a dead person, ten people go and sit in his house to receive comforters.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: A dead person who has no comforters: ten people go and sit in his place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from ideas about the soul to a practical rule about mourning, taught by רב יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We just learned that the soul mourns for seven days. So even a person with no family should not be left without mourning. Ten people take the place of mourners, so that comfort is given in his memory.

keyTerms.meaning: Comforters (here meaning mourners who receive comfort)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical rule about mourning. It shows that the community must care for a dead person even when he has no family.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
A dead person who has no comforters,
phrases.notes: He means there are no mourners there to be comforted.

phrases.english: ten people go
and sit in his place.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה מֵת שֶׁאֵין לוֹ מְנַחֲמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the soul's seven days of mourning to a practical rule about mourning a person who has no family.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a dead person has no mourners, ten people sit in his place to receive comforters.

steps.title: A man died near רב יהודה with no mourners
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts a story: a man died in רב יהודה's neighborhood and had no one to mourn him.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man died in רב יהודה's neighborhood, and he had no comforters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a story that shows רב יהודה's rule in action. The rest of the story continues in the next part of the daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line only sets the scene: a real case that matches the rule from step 35. We should expect to see what רב יהודה did for this man next.

phrases.english: A certain man who died
in Rav Yehuda's neighborhood,
had no comforters,
phrases.notes: The story continues on the next amud

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a story that applies רב יהודה's rule from step 35.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up a real case of a dead man with no mourners, to show how רב יהודה applied his own rule.
